multi-tenant.learn: Resolve tenant identity once, at the request boundary (middleware/guard) — never re-derive it inside business logic, and never trust a client-supplied tenant id without validating the caller's authority to use it.
multi-tenant.why: Cross-tenant data leaks are the single most damaging bug class in B2B SaaS — the kind that ends a customer relationship, not just a sprint.
checklist: Explain, from memory, where tenant context gets resolved in this codebase and why it happens before business logic
Name a concrete way a client could try to smuggle another tenant's id into a request, and how the guard stops it
Explain how impersonation can override tenant scoping safely without becoming a backdoor

permissions.learn: Design permissions as capabilities — resource, action, and scope — and treat roles as configurable bundles of them. Never branch business logic on a role name.
permissions.why: Access-control design is one of the fastest tells of engineering seniority — juniors hardcode role checks, seniors design a vocabulary that survives the customer renaming their org chart.
permissions.youtubeLabel: RBAC vs. ABAC: Which Should You Use?
checklist: Explain why `if (user.role === 'Manager')` in business logic is a code smell
Say when you'd reach for scope-based (ABAC) checks instead of plain role checks
Explain why hiding a UI element is not the same as enforcing access, and where real enforcement must live

state-machine.learn: Before building a multi-step flow, write down the states and the allowed transitions between them explicitly — don't let the UI infer state from a pile of booleans.
state-machine.why: Most 'edge case' bugs in real products are just states nobody named. Naming them turns a bug hunt into a checklist.
state-machine.youtubeLabel: XState - An Introduction: Finite State Machines in React
checklist: List the states of one real flow in this codebase (exam attempt or approval) from memory
Explain why idempotent submission matters and how you'd guarantee it
Explain the difference between a status label and a state machine

transactions.learn: Draw the transaction boundary around the business action the user expects to be atomic (e.g. 'register' = credentials + profile + role), not around whichever repository calls happen to sit next to each other.
transactions.why: Partial writes create the support tickets nobody can reproduce — 'my account is broken' three weeks later, with no idea why.
transactions.youtubeLabel: Relational Database ACID Transactions (Explained by Example)
checklist: Name a workflow in this codebase that touches 2+ tables and say whether it's currently transactional
Explain what happens to already-issued side effects (emails, tokens) if a transaction rolls back midway
Explain the difference between a database transaction and a 'logical' multi-step workflow that can't be wrapped in one

timers.concept: Timers, state, and reliable timed interfaces
timers.learn: Treat countdown/expiry as domain state with a source of truth, not as a setInterval side-effect — define what happens on reload, on expiry, and on double-submit before writing the UI.
timers.why: A flaky timer is the fastest way to make users distrust a product that handles anything time-sensitive (exams, auctions, holds).
timers.youtubeLabel: How to Make an Accurate and Precise Timer in JavaScript
checklist: Explain where the 'true' remaining time lives in this app: client clock, server timestamp, or both
Explain what happens if the tab is backgrounded or the page reloads mid-countdown
Explain how double-submission on expiry is prevented

optimistic-ui.learn: Update the UI immediately for responsiveness, but keep local confidence and server confirmation as two distinct states — make a failed sync visible and recoverable instead of silently reverting.
optimistic-ui.why: This is the difference between an app that feels fast and an app that lies to users about whether their data actually saved.
optimistic-ui.youtubeLabel: Optimistic Updates — React/TanStack Query Series, Part 11
checklist: Explain how this app distinguishes 'shown as saved' from 'confirmed saved'
Describe what the user sees when an optimistic update fails to persist
Explain why the server's state must remain the authority even when the UI moved first

exam-design.concept: Hierarchical data, conditional validation, and UX state
exam-design.learn: When data is hierarchical (a passage with child questions) or conditional (a field that depends on another), centralize the traversal/validation rule in one place instead of letting every screen reinvent it.
exam-design.why: This generalizes past exams — any nested or conditional data model (menus, org charts, forms) breaks the same way if the recursive rule isn't written down once.
exam-design.youtubeLabel: How to Handle Form Validation in React: Validate Inputs, Show Errors, Improve UX
checklist: Explain how progress is counted for a question with children — roots only, or leaves?
Name one conditional field in this app and explain what clears it when its condition becomes false
Explain where 'small' UI state (like a review flag) should live so it survives navigation

url-state.learn: Decide state placement by how long the user expects it to survive: ephemeral UI (a drawer) stays local; anything the user expects a refresh, back-button, or shared link to preserve belongs in the URL.
url-state.why: Getting this wrong is invisible in a demo and infuriating in real use — the classic 'I refreshed and lost my filters' complaint.
url-state.youtubeLabel: STOP Using useState — Put State in the URL (React & Next.js)
checklist: Name one piece of state in this app that lives in the URL and explain why it belongs there
Name one piece of state that stays local and explain why it shouldn't be in the URL
Explain what breaks if a shareable filter is kept only in React state

pagination.concept: Pagination, bounded queries, and scalable lists
pagination.learn: Clamp page/limit at the API boundary so a client can never accidentally request an unbounded result set, and select only the fields a list view actually needs.
pagination.why: This is the boring work that's invisible until the day a customer has 50,000 rows and your endpoint times out in front of them.
pagination.youtubeLabel: API Pagination — Offset and Cursor Pagination Explained (Backend Engineering)
checklist: Explain what stops a client from requesting an unbounded limit on a list endpoint
Explain why list endpoints should select fewer fields than detail endpoints
Name the tradeoff between offset pagination and cursor pagination

n-plus-one.concept: N+1 queries and batched data loading
n-plus-one.learn: Before writing a loop that fetches related data per row, ask what the whole response needs, collect the ids, fetch once, then map in memory.
n-plus-one.why: N+1 is the single most common reason a feature works fine in dev and falls over in production the moment real data volume shows up.
n-plus-one.youtubeLabel: The N+1 Query Problem — Fix This in Your Backend Project
checklist: Spot an N+1 pattern by reading code, without running it
Explain the batched-lookup-map fix in your own words
Explain why this is a 'shape of the question' problem, not a syntax problem

audit.learn: For any workflow where 'who did what and why' matters, record actor, timestamp, action, and reason on every transition — not just the current status.
audit.why: A status field tells you where something is. An audit trail tells you how it got there — and that's what support, compliance, and your future self debugging at 2am actually need.
audit.youtubeLabel: The Best Way to Add Audit Tables to Your Database
checklist: Name a workflow in this codebase where losing the 'why' behind a status change would hurt
List the four things a good audit record captures
Explain the difference between what a state machine enforces and what an audit trail explains

security.concept: Secrets, local services, and secure integrations
security.learn: Never let a token or secret reach the browser — the client calls your backend, your backend holds the credential and calls the third party.
security.why: If a secret can be read by the browser, it's public. This single boundary decision prevents an entire category of breach.
security.youtubeLabel: Environment Variables Explained: Secure Setup for Frontend & Backend
checklist: Name one integration in this app and confirm its credential never touches the frontend
Explain why an .env file being gitignored isn't sufficient on its own
Explain where trust begins and ends for a third-party integration in this system

oauth.concept: OAuth, PKCE, token refresh, and revocation
oauth.learn: The first access token is the start of an integration's lifecycle, not the end — plan for callback/state validation, refresh-token rotation, revocation, and a clear disconnected state.
oauth.why: Most OAuth bugs show up weeks later as silent failures (expired tokens nobody refreshed) rather than at integration time, which makes them expensive to trace.
oauth.youtubeLabel: OAuth Is Broken Without This — Meet PKCE
checklist: Explain what PKCE protects against and why it matters even for confidential clients
Explain what happens in this app when a refresh token rotates: is the old one discarded?
Describe what a 'disconnected' integration state looks like to the user

typescript.learn: Put the type-safety work at boundaries — unwrap transport envelopes (success/message/data) once in the API layer so feature code only ever sees the real domain type.
typescript.why: Types are cheapest to get right at the edges of a system; retrofitting them after uncertainty has leaked into twenty components is expensive.
checklist: Find one place in this app where an API envelope is unwrapped, and explain why it's not done in every component instead
Explain the difference between a type that describes wire data and a type that describes domain data
Give an example of a bug that a boundary type would have caught before runtime

react-state.concept: React state, effects, and component design
react-state.learn: Extract a shared component only when it protects a decision (how statuses are colored, how filters collapse) that people would otherwise reimplement inconsistently — not just to deduplicate markup.
react-state.why: Premature abstraction is as expensive as duplication — it hides the decision behind an API that's harder to change than the copy-paste would have been.
react-state.youtubeLabel: State in React — Thinking in React
checklist: Name a shared component in this codebase and the decision it protects
Explain the difference between 'reused markup' and 'reused meaning'
Describe when you'd inline a component back out of a shared library

browser-permissions.concept: Camera, microphone, and browser permission UX
browser-permissions.learn: Treat browser device APIs (camera, mic) as unreliable external services — design for denied, unsupported, interrupted, and revoked states, and always release the stream on cleanup.
browser-permissions.why: The permission grant is the easy 10% of the flow. The failure states are the feature, and they're the part users actually remember.
browser-permissions.youtubeLabel: Mastering getUserMedia in WebRTC — Avoiding Permission Pitfalls
checklist: List the failure states this app's camera flow handles, from memory
Explain what happens to the camera stream when the modal closes
Explain why a permission prompt alone isn't 'done'

quality.concept: Testing, linting, build checks, and feedback loops
quality.learn: Run the cheapest test that could disprove your change immediately after making it — build, lint, and test the touched behavior in a tight loop, not as one giant pass at the end.
quality.why: Short feedback loops are what let you move fast without a growing pile of undiagnosed regressions — this is the actual mechanism behind 'senior engineers ship faster.'
quality.youtubeLabel: Shorten the Feedback Loop — Developer Experience & System Design (PlatformCon 2023)
checklist: Describe your own change -> build -> lint -> test loop in one sentence
Explain why testing at the end of a big refactor gives failures less diagnostic value
Name one part of a project's documented quality loop you don't currently follow

s3-upload.learn: Resize and compress images on the client with a canvas before upload — bound the dimensions and quality so a 10MB photo becomes tens of KB before it ever hits the network.
s3-upload.why: This is a rare case where a small frontend change (not infra spend) fixes a cost problem, a latency problem, and a UX problem simultaneously.
s3-upload.youtubeLabel: Resize & Compress Images in JavaScript (Client Side)
checklist: Explain, from memory, the resize-then-toBlob pipeline this app uses before upload
Say what quality/dimension bounds this app targets and why those numbers
Explain why this is cheaper than a server-side or Lambda-based resizer

pwa.concept: Progressive Web Apps and install prompt handling
pwa.learn: Don't assume `beforeinstallprompt` fires after your component mounts — cache it at the entry point and add delayed retry checks, because browsers fire it on different, unpredictable schedules.
pwa.why: This is a great example of a bug that's invisible in your own browser and real for a meaningful slice of users — the kind that erodes trust in metrics if you don't know to look for it.
pwa.youtubeLabel: Deep Dive into the PWA Install Flow
checklist: Explain why caching the prompt event at the app entry point matters
Name the browsers this app's install hook has to reconcile and how their timing differs
Explain what 'bulletproof' means here — worst case, not happy path

impersonation.concept: Admin impersonation and secure tenant switching
impersonation.learn: Pair a strict backend session/header check with an unmissable visual boundary (a persistent banner) so impersonation is both technically scoped and impossible to forget you're in.
impersonation.why: Impersonation is a feature where the backend being correct isn't enough — the human forgetting they're impersonating is the actual risk, and only UX design fixes that.
checklist: Explain how this app's backend scopes an impersonated session separately from a normal one
Describe the visual cue that makes impersonation impossible to forget
Explain what the 'exit impersonation' path guarantees

nestjs.concept: NestJS services, guards, and centralized business rules
nestjs.learn: When the same rule (e.g. 'is this record frozen') would otherwise be checked in every controller, centralize it in one injectable service and make every write path pass through it.
nestjs.why: Scattered checks are the #1 way a rule silently stops being enforced somewhere — someone adds a new endpoint and nobody tells them the check existed.
nestjs.youtubeLabel: NestJS Authorization: RBAC, ABAC, Claims-Based, and More
checklist: Name a centralized rule in this backend (e.g. FreezeService) and the write paths it protects
Explain what happens if a new controller forgets to call it
Explain the difference between a guard and a service-level check, and when you'd use each
